probes.support_reason: F-1: every numbered sub-requirement is delivered. (1) `fn mid(v: &Vec<i32>) -> i32 { v[1] }` is a function with one parameter of Rust's normal growable-integer-sequence type (`Vec<i32>`, std `alloc::vec::Vec`) whose body returns the element at index 1. (2) `let xs = vec![1, 2, 3];` binds a local to such a sequence containing 1, 2, 3. (3) `let y = mid(&xs);` binds the call's result in Rust's normal binding form. (4) the block's tail expression `y` is the enclosing function's value, which is Rust's normal spelling of 'return y' (Reference, 'Block expressions'). F-2: language and bundled std only. F-3: builds and runs under the frozen recipe unmodified and prints 2, the element at index 1. F-4: no extra flag, package or code generation. F-6: no clause of the Rust Reference or of the std documentation places `Vec`, shared references, the `vec!` macro or indexing under a normative prohibition or deprecation. R10 form selection: the parameter form `&Vec<i32>` (19 tokens for the definition) was measured rather than the 18-token by-value `v: Vec<i32>`, because R2 filters before R10 and a by-value growable-sequence parameter used only to read one element would consume the caller's vector, which is not what a professional Rust author writes (The Rust Programming Language, ch. 4.2 'References and Borrowing': a reference is used to let a function use a value without taking ownership). The equally-18-token `v: &[i32]` was rejected under R1, not R10: a slice is not the growable-sequence type the canonical task names, so writing it would substitute a weaker mechanism (P-a) and cost the probe its FULL.

V2 - `Vec` and `vec!` resolve to items declared outside the fragment. Both names are unqualified prelude names, and Rust Reference, 'Names: Preludes' lets an item in scope shadow a prelude name; the fragment nowhere writes `std::vec::Vec`. The element access, the allocation behaviour and the result are then arbitrary: A8 changes from 'one heap allocation' to 'none observable' and the observable result changes. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/rust/chunk_B/f06p1_V2_shadow.rs: a module-level `struct Vec<T> { items: [T; 3] }` with an `Index` impl and a `macro_rules! vec` that adds 10 to each element; the fragment is byte-identical, builds under the frozen recipe and prints 12 instead of 2. V3 - `i32` resolves to a user type alias for another primitive integer type. `i32` is not a keyword in Rust; it is a name in the language prelude that a module-level item shadows (Reference, 'Names: Preludes'). With `type i32 = u32;` the same fragment produces an unsigned 32-bit result - materially different on dimension 8 (signedness of the value produced). probes.support_reason: F-1: every numbered sub-requirement is delivered. (1) `fn divmod2(a: i32, b: i32) -> (i32, i32) { (a / b, a % b) }` takes two signed 32-bit parameters and produces both the quotient and the remainder from a single call using Rust's normal multiple-result mechanism, the tuple (Rust Reference, 'Tuple types'; tuples are the language's ordinary way to return more than one value and need no declaration). (2) `let (q, r) = divmod2(7, 3);` binds the two results to two separate local names in one binding construct, a tuple pattern (Reference, 'Tuple patterns'). (3) `q + r` is the enclosing function's value. F-2: language only, no std item is used. F-3: builds and runs under the frozen recipe and prints 3 (7/3 = 2, 7%3 = 1). F-4: nothing beyond the frozen recipe. F-6: no normative prohibition or deprecation applies to tuples, tuple patterns or the arithmetic operators. R10 form selection: the tuple form (28 tokens for the definition; 45 for the whole fragment) was measured against a two-field record - `struct DivMod { q: i32, r: i32 }` with its construction and two field reads, a 57-token fragment - and against out-parameters `fn divmod2(a: i32, b: i32, q: &mut i32, r: &mut i32)`, a 69-token fragment that also fails sub-requirement (2), since the two results would not be bound by one binding construct. The tuple is both the fewest-token form and the form the Reference presents first for multiple results.
